tagline: The old Post Road passes a parish green and evolving colonial houses
intro: Madison’s scenic stretch of US 1 runs 2.34 miles between Neck Road and Lover’s Lane. Along the Boston Post Road, the drive passes a mixed residential and commercial area in western Madison, then the green just west of the commercial strip. Connecticut designated this section a scenic road in 2008. US 1 now primarily serves local businesses, passing the town’s older houses and civic green along a corridor that Interstate 95 parallels.

US 1 generally follows the old Boston Post Road and the turnpike roads that replaced it. Interstate 95 later took over its through-route role, leaving US 1 primarily a local business route. Madison’s green began as the site of the East Guilford parish meetinghouse in 1705; the village center became a town center when Madison incorporated in 1826.

Traveling east from Neck Road, Shelley House at 248 Boston Post Road comes before Madison Green. The green faces a row of eighteenth- and nineteenth-century houses across the Post Road. Just east of the green, the Deacon John Grave House dates to 1681, another saltbox along the Post Road. Farther east, Samson Rock sits between shopping centers and a parking lot, before the scenic stretch ends at Lover’s Lane.

moments.title: Shelley House
moments.text: Shelley House’s long rear roof slopes to the top of the first floor, giving the building its saltbox form. The house grew in stages from a one-room stone ender. Architectural historian J. Frederick Kelly dated the oldest portion, the east room, to the late seventeenth century. Architectural evidence suggests that room and the main chimney came first, followed by rooms to the left in the early eighteenth century and a rear lean-to in mid-century. The exact construction date and original owners’ identities beyond the Shelley name remain unknown. The second story overhangs the first, and the central entrance sits between symmetrically placed sash windows.
moments.notice: The upper story overhangs the lower one, and a large stone chimney rises at the center.

moments.title: Madison Green
moments.text: The First Congregational Church owns the green it faces, but the present church is younger than the green itself. The green was established in 1705 for the meetinghouse of the newly authorized East Guilford parish, when this was part of Guilford. It became Madison’s town center after incorporation in 1826; the present church followed in 1838. Across the Post Road stand eighteenth- and nineteenth-century houses. Three war memorials occupy the green’s southeast corner, while a flagpole marks the center. The memorials distinguish the Revolutionary War and World War I from a shared commemoration of World War II, Korea and Vietnam.
moments.notice: A row of eighteenth- and nineteenth-century houses faces the green across the Boston Post Road.

moments.title: Samson Rock
moments.text: Samson Rock is a glacial erratic boulder set between two shopping centers and a parking lot. A somewhat foot-shaped indentation marks its top. In Algonquin legend, the giant Odziozo dropped the rock while throwing earth into the sea to form Tuxis Island, then stepped on it as he left. European settlers recast the figure as the biblical Samson, giving the boulder its name. A bronze plaque commemorates the legend. The Madison Foundation, Madison Rotary Club and Stop and Shop placed the plaque; a road and a bus stop also carry the rock’s name.
moments.notice: The boulder has a somewhat foot-shaped indentation on top.
